takeaway: FiDe reserves an isolated end-to-end heartbeat path for crash detection, turning tightly bounded jitter into short timeouts and faster failure-aware coordination under explicit synchrony assumptions.
background: Failure detectors let distributed services react when a process stops, commonly by timing out missing heartbeats. Shared processors and networks create long, unpredictable tails, forcing a tradeoff between false suspicions and slow recovery.
villain: A timeout cannot be both short and trustworthy when heartbeat processing and delivery compete unpredictably with ordinary application work.
approach: A per-host kernel module watches local process exits, while a dedicated core sends heartbeats and failure notices through an isolated NIC queue and an XDP/eBPF receive path. An SDN controller assigns priority-treated, rate-limited redundant multicast trees, derives timeouts from bounded path latency and jitter, and repairs a tree after network faults. FiDe also carries bounded application payloads in heartbeats; the authors use that property to build and verify new reliable-broadcast and consensus primitives.
impact: The authors claim that a controlled crash-detection substrate can improve failure-free coordination performance while notifying services quickly when a process actually exits.

evaluation.overview: The authors measure long-run interaction stability, crash-detection latency, Redis and ZooKeeper integrations, network-fault risk, deployment distance, and reserved-resource overhead.
evaluation.implemented: A C implementation split among a Linux kernel module, XDP/eBPF hooks, and a userspace API, plus FiDe-backed Redis consensus modules and ZooKeeper configurations.
evaluation.setting: Experiments used Ethernet servers and redundant paths in an SAP production datacenter, with background CPU and network load; a separate multi-switch testbed examined larger topologies.

results.text: For remote application crashes, FiDe's measured maximum detection latency was 26.54 µs versus 193.56 µs for uKharon-FD, which the authors report as a 7.2× improvement in worst-case latency.
In the failure-free ZooKeeper SET benchmark, the HUC integration achieved up to 2.23× the native throughput and reduced request latency to 0.57× the native value at its best evaluated point.

limitations: FiDe targets crash-stop failures, not gray, fail-slow, partial-software, or Byzantine failures; its HUC and HSUC protocols can stall on a slow but non-crashed participant. Reliability depends on a controlled synchronous FiDe domain with a dedicated active core, isolated receive resources, priority-treated redundant network paths, and end-host rate limits; a sufficiently close compound network failure can violate that model.
phd_group_signal: The work combines OS and network isolation, explicit probabilistic assumptions, formally checked coordination algorithms, long-tail measurement, and application integration rather than treating failure detection as a standalone microbenchmark.

claims.text: FiDe combines kernel-level local-exit observation, a dedicated uninterrupted heartbeat loop, isolated NIC and XDP receive processing, and SDN-configured redundant multicast trees with priority queues and end-host rate limiting.

FiDe's correctness and efficiency depend on synchrony inside its controlled domain; redundant trees and recovery make violations rare rather than impossible, and critical compound network failures can break the assumption.

FiDe directly detects crash-stop process failures; gray, fail-slow, partial-software, and Byzantine failures require another detector or lie outside its model, while HUC and HSUC wait for every non-crashed process.
